entry.title: From clicks to intent: Why SAP SuccessFactors gets stronger in the agent era
entry.content:
There's a phrase making the rounds in customer meetings and blog posts that's worth taking seriously: "death by AI." The argument goes that as AI agents learn to do the work, the software underneath them becomes a commodity — the SaaS suites we've used for years and keep expanding quietly lose their reason to exist.

So it's a fair question to put on the table: does that apply to SAP SuccessFactors?

I've been living with this question for a while, and my answer is a confident no. But I don't want to wave the concern away, because it points at something real — and the response it demands from us is more urgent than "relax, we're fine."

The good, the bad, and the ugly

The good news first: AI doesn't kill SaaS as a category. What it does kill is undifferentiated, UI-centric software — tools that live or die by the screens you navigate and lack three things: depth of data, authority over the process, and gravity within a larger platform. SAP SuccessFactors has all three, so it isn't threatened at the level of existence.

The bad news is that the pressure is still real, and it lands somewhere specific. It's not about functionality. It's about how people interact with the system — and that's the part that's changing fastest.

The ugly part? The work to be ready for it exposes every shortcut we've taken with our data and processes over the years. More on that later.

From clicks to intent

Think about how HR software has worked for the past decade. You log in, you find the right module, you navigate to the right screen, you fill in the right fields. The interface was the product. Mastering the clicks was the skill — even if WalkMe helped you navigate.

That model is changing in front of us. People increasingly want to state a goal, not learn a menu. Instead of navigating three dashboards to find flight risks, a manager asks: "Show me the high-potential employees at risk of leaving my team." Natural language in, business outcome out.

This is exactly what Joule now brings to SAP SuccessFactors. The intent-based, conversational layer isn't a concept on a roadmap anymore — it's how the work gets done. And that reframes everything underneath it. The screens become less important. The system of record beneath them becomes more important, because it's what makes the intent trustworthy.

Why SuccessFactors doesn't just survive — it compounds

Here's the part the "death by AI" narrative misses. An agent is only as good as what it can reason over and act on. Strip away the interface, and the value doesn't disappear — it concentrates in the layer that most people never see.

Data depth. Agents need context to be useful, and useful HR context isn't a snapshot — it's years of employee history, compensation and performance data, and organization-specific structures. SAP SuccessFactors owns that longitudinal record, now grounded and made machine-readable through the SAP Knowledge Graph. An agent without access to this data is confidently wrong. An agent with it is genuinely helpful.

Process authority. SAP SuccessFactors doesn't just recommend — it approves, audits, documents, and proves compliance. A general-purpose AI tool can draft a suggestion. It can't stand behind a co-determination decision in a German works council, and it can't produce the audit trail your regulators expect. That authority is not a feature. It's the foundation of trust.

Platform gravity. The real advantage isn't any single agent — it's the ground they're built on. With SAP Business Technology Platform and a low-code environment for building and governing agents, the platform becomes the place where AI experiences are created, not just consumed. And because the approach is model-agnostic, you're not locked into one vendor's reasoning engine. You can bring the model you prefer, while the governance, the data, and the process control stay exactly where they belong.

That last point matters more than it first appears. SAP isn't asking you to bet on one frontier model winning the race. The moat was never the model. It's the governed data and the process authority around it.

The winning condition: governed autonomy

The Autonomous HCM vision doesn't mean full autonomy. It means governed autonomy — enough freedom for agents to drive real efficiency, and enough control to keep trust, compliance, and accountability intact.

The clearest way to make that concrete is to be explicit about boundaries. In an HR context, agents may assess risk, justify a recommendation, prepare options, and simulate outcomes. Agents must not finalize compensation, terminate employees, bypass works councils or co-determination, or make legal HR decisions on their own.

Those aren't limitations that hold the technology back. They're the guardrails that make it deployable in the real world — especially in Europe, where the compliance reality your teams live with every day is a genuine competitive advantage, not an obstacle. Generic AI can't honor those rules. A governed HR system can.

The next frontier: governing the agent workforce

Here's where this gets genuinely interesting for those of us in HR. The conversation so far has been about agents doing HR work. The next chapter is HR governing an agent workforce.

As agents scale across your organization, they start to look a lot like a new kind of workforce — one that needs to be mapped into your HR operating model, tied to org units and business functions, and understood in terms of which human skills are affected as the agents take on more. And this reshapes the operating model itself. You don't just need HR business process owners anymore. You need roles that own both the process and the agents that run it — accountable for how the two work together.

Who owns which agent? Which team relies on which capability? How does the workforce shape change as this rolls out? Answering those questions is squarely an HR job. It's the natural extension of everything HR already does well.

So what should you do about it?

If the agent era rewards depth of data, process authority, and platform gravity, then the work to get ready is refreshingly concrete. None of it is exotic. Most of it is discipline.

  1. Move to the cloud — if you haven't already. The agent capabilities described here run in the cloud, and cloud makes everything that follows much easier and faster. If parts of your core HR still runs on-premise, this is the moment to commit to the move. Everything else builds on it.
  2. Fix your data model and your data. Agents amplify whatever they're given. Feed them messy, inconsistent, incomplete data and they'll amplify the mess — faster and more confidently than any human ever could. But clean data starts with a sound model beneath it: clear organizational structures, consistent position management, and a coherent metadata model for how HR data is defined. Get the model right, then get the data clean. That combination is the fuel agents run on.
  3. Build a skills and job architecture foundation. Talent and workforce agents reason over skills. If your skills taxonomy and job architecture are vague or inconsistent, the insight the agents produce will be too.
  4. Standardize and document your processes. Process authority only helps if the processes are actually defined. Agents act on well-designed workflows, not tribal knowledge. Now is the time to capture and standardize how HR work really flows.
  5. Define your autonomy boundaries early. Don't wait for a governance question to become a governance incident. Decide up front what your agents may do, what they must not do, and where a human stays in the loop. Write it down. Involve your works councils.
  6. Invest in AI literacy and change management. The shift from clicks to intent is a shift in how people work. Your teams need to learn to lead agents, not just use software. That's a people challenge before it's a technology one.

The organizations that treat this readiness work as foundational — rather than something to bolt on later — will be the ones that turn the agent era into an advantage instead of anxiety.

What's your take?

Where do you land on this. Are you seeing "death by AI" pressure in your own HR landscape? And here's the question I'd most like your take on: where would you draw the line on what an HR agent is allowed to do?

entry.title: Data Driven Change Management: What Two SAP S/4HANA Programmes Prove About Measuring Adoption
entry.content:
By Anthea Arnol, Change Consultant, Customer Engagement and Adoption ANZ, SAP.

Most organizations running SAP transformations invest in communication, training, and stakeholder engagement. The question that rarely gets answered with evidence is: is it actually working? What are the success factors?

Two Australian state government agencies, one in Queensland and one in New South Wales, tackled this question by deploying structured pulse check surveys before and after their OCM interventions. They measured, intervened, and measured again. The results don't just validate the approach. They show precisely what moves the needle on adoption readiness in SAP cloud programmes, and what doesn't.

This post summarizes the outcomes, identifies the interventions that drove measurable improvement, and offers practical recommendations for SAP project managers, IT leaders, and OCM practitioners running similar programmes.

Why Measuring Change Readiness Matters

Organizational Change Management has a credibility challenge. In many programmes, OCM activities are planned and executed:

  • Newsletters sent
  • Town halls held
  • Training sessions scheduled

Yet the question "did it work?" is often answered with anecdotes rather than data.

Pulse check surveys change that equation. A pulse check is a structured questionnaire deployed at key project milestones to measure:

  • Awareness
  • Understanding
  • Confidence
  • Sentiment

The first round establishes a baseline. The second round, deployed after targeted interventions, tells you whether your change approach is landing and where it isn't.

This shifts OCM from activity reporting ("we sent 14 newsletters and held 6 roadshows") to outcome reporting ("staff understanding increased by 43 points and negative sentiment dropped from 21% to 3%"). For sponsors and steering committees, that's the difference between faith and evidence.

Different cloud deployment models, different team structures, and different levels of OCM resourcing. Yet the same OCM disciplines produced measurable results in both environments. That replicability is one of the most useful findings in the data.

What the Surveys Measured and What Improved

Both programmes measured comparable dimensions:

  • Project awareness
  • Understanding of impact
  • Information access
  • Communication effectiveness
  • Manager support
  • Change readiness
  • Confidence

Both showed improvements across all measured dimensions between Survey 1 and Survey 2.

 

The largest gains came from sentiment. People shifted from uncertainty to confidence. The drivers were:

  • Team-level "What This Means For You" communications
  • Myth-busting fact sheets that replaced speculation with verified information

Communication negative responses dropped from 21% at Survey 1 to just 3% at Survey 2. That shift came from:

  • A structured fortnightly email cadence
  • Change Champion reinforcement across the Finance Directorate

 

NSW started from a lower baseline and achieved the most dramatic improvements. The single largest gain, 57 points in manager support, came from equipping managers with:

  • A one-pager covering key messages
  • FAQs
  • Escalation paths

Information access moved from 13% to 63% after the team created:

  • One centralised SharePoint page
  • Clear headings
  • A bookmarkable link
  • Consistent embedding of the URL in project communications

People can't engage with a project they can't find.

The Interventions That Drove Real Results

Looking across both programmes, six categories of intervention consistently drove measurable improvements.

1. Manager Enablement (Highest Impact)

The approach was consistent:

  • Talking points
  • FAQs
  • Structured manager briefings
  • Team-specific impact information

NSW's +57 point uplift in manager support was the largest single-dimension gain across either programme. Queensland achieved 88% senior leader support at Survey 2 through visible executive endorsement and consistent leadership messaging.

The insight: managers are the highest-leverage channel in any SAP transformation.

2. Single Source of Truth

NSW improved information access by creating a dedicated SharePoint page featuring:

  • What's Changing
  • FAQs
  • Key Dates

Queensland similarly centralised project resources on SharePoint with visible "last updated" indicators and cross-stream links.

The principle: remove information friction before launching engagement activities.

3. Structured Communication Cadence

Both agencies established predictable communication rhythms:

  • Fortnightly project update emails
  • Monthly change newsletters
  • Scheduled management briefings

The key isn't communication volume. It's consistency.

4. Change Champion Networks

Both programmes activated change champion networks to:

  • Cascade messages
  • Create trusted team-level touchpoints
  • Extend communication reach
  • Reinforce key messages locally

Queensland refreshed its Champion forum with structured agendas including:

  • Report Back segments
  • Key messages to cascade
  • Business Readiness updates

5. Concrete Benefits Messaging

NSW's confidence in project success grew from 23% to 58% after the team introduced:

  • Before-and-after process examples
  • Practical demonstrations of future-state ways of working

Abstract statements don't convert uncertain people. Concrete examples do.

6. Feedback Loops

Both agencies implemented:

  • "You Asked / We Did" mechanisms
  • Visible responses to staff concerns
  • Ongoing feedback channels

Closing the feedback loop reduces reliance on rumour and informal networks while building trust in the formal change programme.

Practical Recommendations for SAP Change Programmes

  • Start with measurement. Deploy a baseline pulse check early in your programme. Without it, you're guessing where to invest your OCM effort.
  • Equip managers before anything else - e.g. a one-pager with talking points, 5-6 FAQs, Guidance on where to direct questions can be more effective than any all-staff email campaign.
  • Build information infrastructure first: Create a single, findable, up-to-date source of truth before launching engagement campaigns. Embed the link everywhere.
  • Commit to a communication cadence and maintain it: Fortnightly or monthly, pick a rhythm and don't break it. Consistency matters more than frequency.
  • Show, don't tell: Replace abstract benefit statements with concrete process comparisons.
  • Close the loop visibly: Respond publicly to concerns and demonstrate what changed as a result.
  • Measure again: Deploy Survey 2 after interventions have had time to land. Compare. Report. Adjust.

What This Means for Data-Driven OCM: These two programmes demonstrate that structured OCM practice is both replicable and measurable.

Across different Organisational contexts, Project scopes, Cloud deployment models, OCM resourcing levels, the same disciplines consistently improved readiness:

  • Manager enablement
  • Communication cadence
  • Single source of truth
  • Feedback loops
  • Benefits messaging

The intensity of support matters less than the consistency and structure of the interventions applied.

entry.title: SAP RISE Brownfield Migration – der pragmatische Weg in die Cloud
entry.content:
Einleitung

Viele SAP-Kunden stehen heute vor der Frage: Wie kann eine bestehende SAP-Landschaft in die Cloud gebracht werden, ohne bewährte Prozesse, Daten und Investitionen komplett neu aufzubauen?

Genau hier setzt RISE with SAP an. Für Unternehmen mit einer gewachsenen SAP-Landschaft bietet insbesondere die Brownfield-Transformation einen pragmatischen Weg von SAP ECC oder SAP S/4HANA On-Premise zu SAP Cloud ERP Private. Dabei geht es nicht nur um eine technische Migration, sondern um die schrittweise Modernisierung der gesamten ERP-Landschaft.

Hierzu ein Big Picture mit der SAP RISE Private Cloud Journey

Was bedeutet Brownfield?

Beim Brownfield-Ansatz wird das bestehende SAP-System als Ausgangspunkt genutzt. Daten, Prozesse, Customizing und bestehende Entwicklungen werden weitgehend erhalten und auf ihre Zukunftsfähigkeit geprüft.

Dabei lautet die zentrale Frage nicht:

„Was können wir alles migrieren?“

sondern vielmehr:

„Was wollen wir bewusst in die neue Cloud-Welt mitnehmen?“

Damit verbindet sich die technische System Conversion zunehmend mit dem Clean-Core-Gedanken: unnötige Eigenentwicklungen werden entfernt, bestehende Erweiterungen modernisiert und neue Anforderungen möglichst über Standards, APIs, ABAP Cloud oder SAP BTP umgesetzt.

Welche Migrationswege gibt es?

SAP unterscheidet grundsätzlich mehrere Transition Paths:

1. System Conversion – Brownfield
Das bestehende SAP-System wird technisch auf S/4HANA bzw. SAP Cloud ERP Private überführt. Bestehende Daten und Prozesse können weitgehend erhalten bleiben.

2. Selective Data Transition
Nur ausgewählte Daten, Organisationseinheiten oder Zeiträume werden übernommen. Dieser Ansatz liegt zwischen Brownfield und Greenfield.

3. New Implementation – Greenfield
Das System wird neu aufgebaut und Prozesse werden stärker an SAP-Standards und Best Practices ausgerichtet.

SAP unterstützt diese verschiedenen Wege inzwischen über das SAP Business Transformation Center.

Wie sieht eine Brownfield-Migration typischerweise aus?

Ein pragmatisches Vorgehen lässt sich in sechs Schritte aufteilen:

1. Analyse
Systemlandschaft, Prozesse, Add-ons, Daten und Eigenentwicklungen analysieren.

2. Readiness
Prüfen, welche Voraussetzungen für S/4HANA und die Cloud erfüllt sind.

3. Custom Code & Clean Core
Z-Programme und Erweiterungen klassifizieren: behalten, ersetzen, modernisieren oder ablösen.

4. Transformation & Conversion
Technische Konvertierung und Datenmigration durchführen.

5. Testing & Cutover
Integration, Prozesse und Daten validieren und den Go-Live vorbereiten.

6. Cloud Betrieb & Continuous Improvement
Nach dem Go-Live beginnt die eigentliche Weiterentwicklung: Clean Core, BTP, Integration, Innovation und kontinuierliche Optimierung.

Welche Methodik und SAP-Tools unterstützen dabei?

Die Toolchain wird zunehmend stärker integriert:

TransformationsstrategieBusiness Transformation Center
Readiness & AnalyseSAP Readiness Check
Custom CodeCustom Code Migration / Analyse
Technische ConversionSoftware Update Manager (SUM), DMO
RISE TransitionRISE with SAP System Transition Workbench
Selektive DatenmigrationLean Selective Data Transition
DatenvalidierungData Transition Validation
Projekt, Testing & ALMSAP Cloud ALM
ArchitekturSAP LeanIX
ProzesseSAP Signavio
PersonenSAP WalkMe

Die RISE with SAP System Transition Workbench bündelt und führt die notwendigen technischen Aktivitäten für eine Transition nach RISE und unterstützt dabei einen standardisierten, geführten Ablauf.
Einen guten SAP Blogpost zur SAP System Transition Workbench gibt es hier: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-sap/introducing-the-rise-with-sap-system-transition-workbench/ba-p/14130250 

Sieben AI Assistenten

Auf der SAP Sapphire 2026 kündigte SAP sieben „Migration and Modernization Assistants“ (Assistenten für Migration und Modernisierung) als Teil einer agentenbasierten Toolchain an. Alle sieben basieren operativ auf SAP Cloud ALM. Ein solcher „Assistent“ vereint mehrere KI-Fähigkeiten und Agenten, die gemeinsam an einer spezifischen Transformationsaufgabe arbeiten.

Hier ist die Liste der sieben Assistenten:

  1.  System Analysis Assistant – Analysiert die bestehende SAP-Landschaft des Kunden (Daten, Anpassungen, kundeneigener Code) und schafft die Datengrundlage für alle anderen Assistenten.
  2. Data Management Assistant – Überwacht, korrigiert und steuert die Datenqualität; identifiziert Inkonsistenzen, führt Ursachenanalysen durch und schlägt Lösungen vor bzw. setzt diese um.
  3. Custom Code Assistant – Stellt sicher, dass kundeneigener Code aus SAP ERP Central Component (ECC) in SAP S/4HANA funktioniert; analysiert Erweiterungen semantisch, empfiehlt Wege zum „Clean Core“ und erstellt technische Spezifikationen.
  4. Configuration Assistant – Konfiguriert SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition vorab unter Nutzung des SAP Enterprise Knowledge Graph, von Best-Practice-Modellen und Kundenanforderungen.
  5. Test Management Assistant – Legt den Testumfang fest, generiert KI-basierte Testfälle aus SAP-Signavio-Prozessmodellen sowie Anforderungen und übergibt diese zur automatisierten Ausführung an Tricentis.
  6. Rollout Assistant – Unterstützt globale Template-Rollouts: vergleicht das SAP-Template mit lokalen Marktprozessen und empfiehlt, ob das Template angepasst oder lokalisiert werden sollte.
  7. Project Management Assistant – Liefert einen faktenbasierten Projektstatus in Echtzeit, delegiert Aufgaben rollenspezifisch und identifiziert Risiken proaktiv.

Unterstützte Technische Brownfield Transition Methoden

Folgende technische Transition Methoden sind unterstützt und können angewendet werden.
Auf der Quellseite / On Premise ist es entscheidend welchen Systemstand und welche DB man einsetzt.

Was ist das eigentliche Ziel von RISE?

Für das Unternehmen steht im Vordergrund, bestehende Investitionen und Geschäftsprozesse zu schützen und gleichzeitig eine modernere, skalierbare ERP-Plattform zu schaffen.

Für SAP bedeutet RISE eine stärkere Verlagerung des ERP-Geschäfts in ein Cloud- und Subskriptionsmodell sowie eine Plattform für kontinuierliche Innovation. SAP positioniert RISE heute als geführten Weg von bestehenden ERP-Systemen zu SAP Cloud ERP Private.

Für SAP-Partner verschiebt sich die Wertschöpfung: Klassische Leistungen rund um Infrastruktur und technischen Betrieb verlieren teilweise an Bedeutung. Gleichzeitig entstehen neue Chancen in Transformation, Architektur, Custom Code, Clean Core, Datenmigration, Integration, BTP, Testing, ALM und Continuous Improvement. SAP betont dabei ausdrücklich die zentrale Rolle seiner Partner bei ERP-Transformationen.

Fazit

Brownfield mit RISE ist mehr als eine technische Migration.

Es geht darum, die bestehende SAP-Landschaft schrittweise zu modernisieren, Bewährtes zu erhalten und gleichzeitig technische Altlasten abzubauen.

Der entscheidende Erfolgsfaktor ist deshalb nicht nur die Frage:

„Wie bekommen wir unser SAP-System in die Cloud?“

Sondern:

„Wie machen wir unser bestehendes SAP-System cloudfähig, standardisierter, integrierter und bereit für kontinuierliche Innovation?“

Genau an dieser Schnittstelle zwischen Transformation, Technologie und Business entsteht für Unternehmen, SAP und Partner der eigentliche Mehrwert von RISE.

entry.title: SAP RISE Brownfield Migration – the pragmatic path to the cloud
entry.content:
Introduction

Many SAP customers today face a key question: How can an existing SAP landscape be moved to the cloud without having to completely rebuild proven processes, data structures, and investments?

This is precisely where RISE with SAP comes in. For companies with an established SAP landscape, the "brownfield" transformation approach, in particular, offers a pragmatic path from SAP ECC or SAP S/4HANA on-premise to SAP Cloud ERP Private. This process involves not merely a technical migration, but the gradual modernization of the entire ERP landscape.

Here is an overview of the SAP RISE Private Cloud Journey

What does "Brownfield" mean?

The Brownfield approach uses the existing SAP system as a starting point. Data, processes, configuration settings, and existing custom developments are largely retained and evaluated for their future viability.

The central question here is not:

"What can we migrate?"

but rather:

"What do we consciously want to carry over into the new cloud world?"

This increasingly links the technical system conversion with the "Clean Core" concept: unnecessary custom developments are removed, existing extensions are modernized, and new requirements are implemented—wherever possible—using standard features, APIs, ABAP Cloud, or SAP BTP.

What migration paths are available?

SAP generally distinguishes between several transition paths:

1. System Conversion – Brownfield
The existing SAP system is technically converted to S/4HANA or SAP Cloud ERP Private. Existing data and processes can largely be retained.

2. Selective Data Transition
Only selected data, organizational units, or time periods are transferred. This approach falls between Brownfield and Greenfield.

3. New Implementation – Greenfield
The system is built from scratch, and processes are more closely aligned with SAP standards and best practices.

SAP now supports these various paths via the SAP Business Transformation Center.

What does a brownfield migration typically look like?

A pragmatic approach can be broken down into six steps:

1. Analysis
Analyze the system landscape, processes, add-ons, data, and custom developments.

2. Readiness
Check which prerequisites for S/4HANA and the cloud are met.

3. Custom Code & Clean Core
Classify custom programs and extensions: keep, replace, modernize, or retire.

4. Transformation & Conversion
Execute technical conversion and data migration.

5. Testing & Cutover
Validate integration, processes, and data, and prepare for go-live.

6. Cloud Operations & Continuous Improvement
The actual ongoing development begins after go-live: Clean Core, BTP, integration, innovation, and continuous optimization.

Which methodology and SAP tools support this?

The toolchain is becoming increasingly integrated:

TransformationstrategyBusiness Transformation Center
Readiness & AnalyseSAP Readiness Check
Custom CodeCustom Code Migration / Analyse
Technical ConversionSoftware Update Manager (SUM), DMO
RISE TransitionRISE with SAP System Transition Workbench
Selective Data MigrationLean Selective Data Transition
DatavalidationData Transition Validation
Project, Testing & ALMSAP Cloud ALM
ArchitectureSAP LeanIX
ProcessesSAP Signavio
PeopleSAP WalkMe

The RISE with SAP System Transition Workbench consolidates and executes the technical activities required for a transition to RISE, supporting a standardized, guided process.
You can find a good SAP blog post about the SAP System Transition Workbench here: LINK

Seven AI Assistants

At SAP Sapphire 2026, SAP announced seven Migration and Modernization Assistants as part of the agent-led toolchain. All seven run on SAP Cloud ALM as the operational foundation. An "Assistant" means multiple AI skills and multiple agents working together on a specific transformation challenge.

Below is the list of seven assistants:
  • System Analysis Assistant - Scans the customer's existing SAP landscape - data, customizations, custom code - and builds the data foundation for all other assistants.
  • Data Management Assistant - Monitors, corrects, and governs data quality; identifies inconsistencies, performs root cause analysis, and proposes and implements fixes.
  • Custom Code Assistant - Ensures SAP ERP Central Component (ECC) custom code runs in SAP S/4HANA; semantically analyzes extensions, recommends clean core paths, generates technical specifications.
  • Configuration Assistant - Pre-configures SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition using SAP's Enterprise Knowledge Graph, best practice models, and customer requirements.
  • Test Management Assistant - Scopes testing, generates AI test cases from SAP Signavio process models and requirements, and hands off to Tricentis for automated execution.
  • Rollout Assistant - For global template rollouts: compares the SAP template against local market processes and recommends whether to adapt the template or localize.
  • Project Management Assistant - Provides real-time, fact-based project status, delegates tasks by persona, and identifies risks proactively.

Supported Technical Brownfield Transition Methods

The following technical transition methods are supported and can be used.
On the source side (on-premise), the system version and database being used are critical factors.

What is the primary goal of RISE?

For the company, the priority is to protect existing investments and business processes while simultaneously creating a more modern, scalable ERP platform.

For SAP, RISE represents a significant shift of the ERP business toward a cloud and subscription model, as well as a platform for continuous innovation. SAP currently positions RISE as a guided path from existing ERP systems to SAP Cloud ERP Private.

For SAP partners, the value proposition is shifting: traditional services related to infrastructure and technical operations are becoming less significant in some areas. At the same time, new opportunities are emerging in transformation, architecture, custom code, "Clean Core," data migration, integration, BTP, testing, ALM, and continuous improvement. In this context, SAP explicitly emphasizes the pivotal role its partners play in ERP transformations.

Conclusion

A brownfield approach with RISE is more than just a technical migration.

It is about gradually modernizing the existing SAP landscape, preserving what works well, and simultaneously reducing technical debt.

The decisive success factor, therefore, is not merely the question:

“How do we get our SAP system into the cloud?”

But rather:

“How do we make our existing SAP system cloud-ready, more standardized, more integrated, and prepared for continuous innovation?”

It is precisely at this intersection of transformation, technology, and business that the true value of RISE emerges for companies, SAP, and partners.

entry.title: Business AI in ABAP Cloud - Embedding AI with the ABAP AI SDK (Part 2)
entry.content:
Business AI in ABAP Cloud - Embedding AI with the ABAP AI SDK (Part 2)

Cheers ABAP Folks!

In my last blog post, we discussed the high-level strategy for implementing business AI capabilities in ABAP Cloud. We looked at the two pillars, Embedded AI in ABAP and Agentic AI via Joule, and when to use which approach. If you haven't read it yet, I'd recommend starting there for the bigger picture.

Today, we're going hands-on. This post dives into Embedded AI, the capabilities that run directly inside your ABAP application, powered by the ABAP AI SDK. We'll walk through the fundamentals, introduce the SDK, and then look at two concrete use cases using everyone's favorite business scenario: Trip & Expense Management.

Yes, trip & expense management. We all love it, don't we? Nothing brings more joy to a business traveler than filling out expense reports after a long trip. So, let's see how AI can take some of that joy... I mean burden... away.

 

 

The Fundamentals: Connecting ABAP to AI

Before you write a single line of AI-related ABAP code, you need to get the plumbing right. All embedded AI scenarios in ABAP Cloud require a connection to SAP AI Core, specifically to the Generative AI Hub that provides access to Large Language Models (LLMs) hosted by hyperscalers.

This connection is established via Intelligent Scenario Lifecycle Management (ISLM), a framework that allows you to manage and operate AI scenarios in a standardized, transportable way. Think of ISLM as the lifecycle backbone: it handles connectivity, model deployment, prompt management, and the runtime configuration that ties everything together.

Setting Up the Connection

The setup follows a straightforward pattern (SAP Help, Set Up ABAP AI SDK powered by ISLM)

  1. Subscribe to SAP AI Core in your SAP BTP subaccount and enable the required service plan.
  2. Create a service instance and service key for SAP AI Core in the BTP cockpit.
  3. Establish connectivity between SAP AI Core and your ABAP system by creating a communication arrangement based on communication scenario SAP_COM_0A69.

This is a customer-managed outbound integration, which means you own the connection setup. Once established, ISLM can create and activate model deployments, and the ABAP AI SDK can execute prompts against the deployed models. For a detailed step-by-step walkthrough, I recommend the tutorial Set Up SAP BTP and Integrate SAP AI Core with ISLM on SAP Developers.

The ABAP AI SDK, Your AI Toolbox

With the connection established, let's talk about the tool you'll actually use in your ABAP code: the ABAP AI SDK. It's a typed, ABAP-native reuse library that provides access to generative AI functionality via ISLM. It is available across the full ABAP Cloud landscape, covering:

  • SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition & On-Premise
  • SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition
  • SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment (Steampunk)

This means the same SDK, the same APIs, the same patterns, regardless of where your ABAP system runs.

What's in for me?

The ABAP AI SDK offers a set of APIs built around common LLM usage patterns:

  • Completion API – Send a prompt to an LLM and receive a generated text response. This is the core building block for most embedded AI scenarios.
  • Prompt Library API – Work with prompt templates predefined in ISLM, including parameterized prompts with runtime variable substitution. Very useful when you want to keep your prompts maintainable and out of your ABAP code.
  • Connectivity management – The SDK handles the connection to the Generative AI Hub transparently. You reference an intelligent scenario by name, and the SDK resolves the rest.
  • Exception handling – Typed ABAP exceptions, so you can integrate AI calls into your existing error handling patterns without reinventing the wheel.

The APIs are vendor-neutral, meaning the same ABAP code works regardless of which underlying LLM provider is configured in SAP AI Core. If your organization switches from one model to another, you change the configuration in ISLM, not your ABAP code. Your CTO changes their mind about the AI vendor? No problem, no code change required – ok, to be honest with you: The prompting might be polished most probably a little.

The Simplest Possible Call

To give you a feel for the developer experience, here's the simplest possible AI call using the Completion API (SAP ABAP Cheat Sheets, Generative AI)

" Get a Completion API instance for your intelligent scenario
DATA(ai_api) = cl_aic_islm_compl_api_factory=>get( )->create_instance( 'Z_MY_SCENARIO' ).

" Execute a prompt and get the result
DATA(result) = ai_api->execute_for_string( `Classify this trip as customer-facing or internal.` ).

" Retrieve the generated text
DATA(completion) = result->get_completion( ).

Three lines of ABAP. That's it. The factory creates an instance tied to your intelligent scenario (which contains all the connection and model details), you execute a prompt, and you get back the LLM's response as a string. No HTTP client setup, no JSON parsing, no authentication handling. The SDK takes care of all of that. If you've ever tried calling a REST API from ABAP the "old-fashioned way", you'll know exactly how much boilerplate this saves you.

Of course, real-world scenarios are a bit more involved. You'll use prompt templates with parameters, handle exceptions, and integrate the result into your business logic. But the fundamental pattern stays the same.

Orchestration Capabilities

For enterprise-grade AI scenarios, the ABAP AI SDK also supports orchestration through the SAP AI Core Orchestration Service. This adds capabilities that are critical for production use:

  • Data Masking – Automatically redact sensitive information (personal data, financial details) before it reaches the LLM. Essential for data protection and GDPR compliance, and something your compliance team will thank you for.
  • Document Grounding – Enrich your prompts with business-relevant context from documents, reducing hallucinations and improving response accuracy. Because an LLM that confidently makes things up is entertaining at dinner parties, but not in your ERP system.
  • Content Filtering – Ensure that LLM responses are safe, appropriate, and compliant with your organisation's policies.

These capabilities are configured at the orchestration level, so you don't need to implement masking or filtering logic yourself in ABAP. It's handled for you.

 

Let’s get our hands dirty: Trip & Expense Management

For the rest of this blog post, we'll use a Trip & Expense Management application as our running example. Picture a RAP-based Fiori application where employees create travel requests, and after the trip, submit expense reports.

We'll tackle two concrete use cases:

  1. Data Prediction with Fiori Input Assistance: Automatically categorizing a trip as "customer-facing" or "internal" based on the trip description.
  2. Data Extraction from files:  Extracting structured data (payment amounts, categories, etc.) from uploaded receipt documents.

Both are real-world scenarios that demonstrate different facets of the ABAP AI SDK. And both address the same fundamental truth: nobody enjoys filling out forms manually when a machine could do it better and faster. Let's start.

 

Use Case 1: Trip Categorization with RAP Recommendations

The Problem

When an employee creates a travel request, they need to fill out several fields: destination, purpose, cost center, and importantly, trip category (e.g. "customer-facing" or "internal"). This categorization drives downstream processes like approval workflows, budget allocation, and reporting. Today, users pick the category manually. They might get it wrong, or they pick whatever option is closest to the mouse cursor. What if the system could propose the right category automatically, based on the trip description?

The Solution: Fiori Input Assistance

This is exactly what Fiori Input Assistance implemented with RAP recommendations is designed for. RAP recommendations are a built-in input assistance feature in the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP) that proposes field values for input fields on an SAP Fiori UI (SAP Help, Defining RAP Recommendations). Available since SAP BTP ABAP Environment 2602 and SAP S/4HANA Cloud 2602, RAP Recommendations can be implemented using either deterministic rules or generative AI, and you can even mix both approaches in the same application. The key principles of RAP recommendations:

  • They are exposed in SAP Fiori as a recommendation pattern of type input assistance, meaning the user sees suggested values directly in the input field.
  • They are built on top of a value help, so you need an existing value help for the target field.
  • They are triggered by side effects: when the user changes a source field (e.g. trip description), the recommendation function runs and proposes values for the target field (e.g. trip category).
  • They integrate seamlessly with the RAP programming model. No custom UI development required. Zero. Nada.

Figure 1: Fiori Input Assistance implemented with RAP recommendations

How It Works: The Architecture

The implementation involves three layers:

  1. Behavior Definition – Declare which fields receive recommendations and define the recommendation function.
  2. Behavior Implementation – Implement the recommendation logic in the behavior pool, using the ABAP AI SDK to call an LLM for intelligent categorization.
  3. Projection Behavior Definition – Expose the recommendations in the projection layer for the Fiori UI.

If you've built a RAP Business Object before, this will feel very familiar. It's the same layered pattern, just with AI sprinkled on top.

Step 1: Define Recommendations in the Behavior Definition

In your behavior definition, you mark the target field as relevant for recommendations, declare a recommendation function and define a side effect on which the recommendation function should be triggered. This tells the RAP framework: whenever the user changes the “title” field, execute function GetRecommendedValuesFunction and propose values for attribute “type”. The user types "Customer workshop in Berlin" and the system immediately suggests "Customer-facing". It almost feels like the system is reading the user's mind, except it's reading their input field.

define behavior for ZR_AITRIP alias Trip
{
  //Define for which fields an recommendation output is generated
  field ( recommendations ) Type;

  //Define the recommendation function itself
  recommendation function GetRecommendedValuesFunction;

  //Define the trigger (e.g. other context field)
  side effects
  {
    recommendation function GetRecommendedValuesFunction 
      executed on field Title;
  }
}

Step 2: Implement the Recommendation Logic

In the behavior pool, you implement the recommendation function. This is where the ABAP AI SDK comes in. You use the completion API to ask an LLM to categorize the trip based on the available context:

  1. Read the current entity data (description, destination, etc.)
  2. Build a prompt with the trip context, based on your system's master data
  3. Call the ABAP AI SDK Completion API
  4. Parse the LLM response
  5. Return the recommended value(s) with scores

The recommendation function returns a list of proposed values, each with a score and a flag indicating whether it's the suggested (top-ranked) value. The Fiori UI renders these as input assistance. The user can accept, modify, or override the suggestion. The AI proposes, the human decides. As it should be.

The full implementation:

class lhc_zr_aitrip definition inheriting from cl_abap_behavior_handler.

  private section.

    methods get_global_authorizations for global authorization
      importing
        request requested_authorizations for Trip
        result  result.

    methods GetRecommendedValuesFunction for read
      keys for function Trip~GetRecommendedValuesFunction result result.

    methods build_recommendation_prompt
      importing title         type string
      returning value(result) type string.

    methods get_type_recommendation
      importing prompt        type string
      returning value(result) type string.

endclass.


class lhc_zr_aitrip implementation.

  method get_global_authorizations.
    " demo only: open for all users - add real authorization checks before productive use
    result-%create = if_abap_behv=>auth-allowed.
  endmethod.

  method GetRecommendedValuesFunction.

    result = corresponding #( keys ).

    read entities of zr_aitrip in local mode
      entity Trip
        fields ( Title ) with corresponding #( keys )
      result data(trips)
      failed failed.

    loop at result assigning field-symbol(<result>).

      read table trips with table key id components %tky = <result>-%tky into data(trip).
      check sy-subrc = 0 and trip-Title is not initial.

      data(type_prompt)      = build_recommendation_prompt( conv #( trip-Title ) ).
      data(recommended_type) = get_type_recommendation( type_prompt ).

      check recommended_type is not initial.

      <result>-%param = value #(
        trip-type = value #( (
          score     = '1.0'
          value     = recommended_type
          suggested = 'X' ) ) ).

    endloop.

  endmethod.


  method build_recommendation_prompt.

    result = |Derive a trip category based on the given trip title: | &&
             |{ title }| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf &&
             |The following trip categories exist: C (Customer facing), I (Internal).| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf &&
             |Please only answer with 'C' or 'I' as a single character.|.

  endmethod.


  method get_type_recommendation.

    try.
        data(api)                = cl_aic_islm_compl_api_factory=>get( )->create_instance( 'ZINTS_TRAVELAPP' ).
        data(message_container)  = api->create_message_container( ).
        message_container->add_user_message( prompt ).

        result = api->execute_for_messages( message_container )->get_completion( ).

      catch cx_aic_api_factory cx_aic_prompt_template cx_aic_completion_api.
        " recommendations are optional - on failure the field simply gets no suggested value
    endtry.

  endmethod.

endclass.

Step 3: Expose in the Projection

Make sure to expose the functionality in your UI projection by using “use recommendations;”. And that's it. The Fiori UI picks up the recommendation pattern automatically. No custom UI code, no frontend development, no begging a UI5 developer for help.

The Beauty of It

The beauty of RAP recommendations is the zero-effort UX integration. You implement the intelligence once in the behavior pool, and every Fiori Elements UI that consumes your RAP Business Object automatically benefits from the recommendations. It's the RAP philosophy at its finest: define the behavior, and the framework handles the presentation. And because the recommendation logic uses the ABAP AI SDK, you can switch from a deterministic rule-based approach to a generative AI approach (or vice versa) without changing the behavior definition or the UI. The abstraction is clean, the separation of concerns is real, and your future self will thank your present self for the architecture.

 

Use Case 2: Receipt Data Extraction

The Problem

After a business trip, the employee needs to submit expense reports with receipts attached. Hotel invoices, restaurant bills, taxi receipts. Today, the employee manually types in every field: vendor name, amount, currency, date, tax, category. It's tedious, error-prone, and, let's be honest, the reason most people procrastinate on their expense reports for weeks. Some of us have receipts from trips that happened so long ago that the ink has faded. Not speaking from personal experience, of course.

What if the employee could simply upload a receipt image and the system would extract the relevant data automatically?

Figure 2: AI-generated invoice

The Solution: Document Extraction with the ABAP AI SDK

This use case leverages the ABAP AI SDK's ability to send content, including file-based content, to an LLM and receive structured data back. The flow is:

  1. The user uploads a receipt (image) through the Fiori application.
  2. The ABAP application receives the file content.
  3. The ABAP AI SDK sends the file content along with a structured prompt to the LLM (via the Generative AI Hub).
  4. The LLM extracts key fields: vendor name, amount, currency, date, tax amount, expense category.
  5. The extracted data is returned to the ABAP application and pre-fills the expense line item.

The user uploads a crumpled taxi receipt, and five seconds later all the fields are filled in correctly. That's the kind of user experience that makes people actually submit their expense reports on time.

Figure 3: Extracted data from file

Step 1: Enhance the CDS Data Model for File Upload

Before we can extract anything, we need to give users a way to upload their receipts. In RAP, file uploads are modelled as Large Objects (LOBs) using the @Semantics.largeObject annotation in your CDS view. This tells the framework to treat the field as a binary stream and render it as a file upload control in the Fiori UI (SAP Help, Working with Large Objects). First, your database table needs three fields: the binary content itself, a MIME type field, and a file name field. Then, in your CDS entity, you annotate them accordingly:

@Semantics.largeObject: {
    acceptableMimeTypes: [ 'image/*', 'application/*' ],
    cacheControl.maxAge: #MEDIUM,
    contentDispositionPreference: #INLINE,
    fileName: 'UploadedReceiptFileName',
    mimeType: 'UploadedReceiptMimeType'
}
UploadedReceipt,

@Semantics.mimeType: true
UploadedReceiptMimeType,

UploadedReceiptFileName,

Let's break down what's happening here:

  • UploadedReceipt is the actual LOB field that stores the binary content of the uploaded file. The @Semantics.largeObject annotation binds it to its MIME type and file name fields, and defines which file types are accepted.
  • acceptableMimeTypes controls what the user can upload. In our case, image/* covers photos of receipts (JPEG, PNG, etc.) and application/* covers PDFs and other document formats. If you want to be more restrictive, you can specify individual MIME types like 'image/jpeg', 'application/pdf'.
  • UploadedReceiptMimeType stores the MIME type of the uploaded file and must carry the @Semantics.mimeType: true annotation. This is what the framework uses to know how to handle the file.
  • UploadedReceiptFileName stores the original file name. Technically optional, but very much recommended, because your users will appreciate seeing "taxi_receipt_berlin.pdf" instead of a cryptic binary blob identifier.
  • contentDispositionPreference: #INLINE tells the browser to display the file directly when possible (e.g. images and PDFs), rather than forcing a download.

Once these annotations are in place, the Fiori Elements automatically renders an upload control on the Object Page. No UI5 coding, no custom frontend logic. The user clicks upload, picks a file, and the binary content flows into your RAP Business Object. If you've ever implemented file upload the "classic" way in SAP, you'll appreciate how clean this is.

Step 2: Extract Data with the ABAP AI SDK

With the receipt uploaded and stored in the LOB field, the extraction can begin. The implementation combines the file content from the RAP entity with the ABAP AI SDK Completion API. You read the binary content from the LOB, and send it along with a structured extraction prompt through the SDK.

An execution flow could look like this:

  1. Read the uploaded receipt content from the entity (UploadedReceipt field)
  2. Convert to base64 encoding
  3. Build a structured extraction prompt:    
    'Extract the following fields from this receipt: vendor_name, amount, currency, date, tax_amount, category. Return the result as JSON'.
  4. Call the ABAP AI SDK Completion API with the prompt and the file content
  5. Parse the JSON response
  6. Map extracted fields to the expense line item entity

The full implementation:

class lhc_expense definition inheriting from cl_abap_behavior_handler.

  private section.

    types: begin of ty_reference_lists,
             transaction_types type string,
             categories        type string,
           end of ty_reference_lists.

    methods extractData for determine on modify
      keys for Expense~extractData.

    methods get_reference_data_lists
      returning value(result) type ty_reference_lists.

    methods build_extraction_prompt
      importing reference_lists type ty_reference_lists
      returning value(result)   type string.

    methods call_ai_extraction
      importing receipt       type xstring
                prompt        type string
      returning value(result) type string
      raising   cx_aic_completion_api
                cx_aic_api_factory.

    methods parse_extraction_response
      importing json    type string
      changing  expense type any
      raising   cx_root.

endclass.


class lhc_expense implementation.

  method extractData.

    read entities of zr_aitrip in local mode
         entity Expense all fields with corresponding #( keys )
         result data(expenses).

    check expenses is not initial.

    data(reference_lists) = get_reference_data_lists( ).
    data(prompt)          = build_extraction_prompt( reference_lists ).

    data updates type table for update zr_aitrip\\Expense.

    loop at expenses assigning field-symbol(<expense>).

      if <expense>-UploadedReceipt is initial.
        append value #( %tky = <expense>-%tky
                         %msg = new_message_with_text( severity = if_abap_behv_message=>severity-error
                                                        text     = 'No receipt uploaded - nothing to extract' ) )
          to reported-expense.
        continue.
      endif.

      try.
          data(answer) = call_ai_extraction( receipt = <expense>-UploadedReceipt
                                              prompt  = prompt ).

          parse_extraction_response( exporting json    = answer
                                      changing  expense = <expense> ).

          append corresponding #( <expense> ) to updates.

        catch cx_aic_completion_api cx_aic_api_factory into data(ai_error).
          append value #( %tky = <expense>-%tky
                           %msg = new_message_with_text( severity = if_abap_behv_message=>severity-error
                                                          text     = |Receipt could not be processed by the AI service: { ai_error->get_text( ) }| ) )
            to reported-expense.

        catch cx_root into data(parse_error).
          append value #( %tky = <expense>-%tky
                           %msg = new_message_with_text( severity = if_abap_behv_message=>severity-error
                                                          text     = |Receipt data could not be interpreted: { parse_error->get_text( ) }| ) )
            to reported-expense.
      endtry.

    endloop.

    check updates is not initial.

    modify entities of zr_aitrip in local mode
       entity Expense
       update fields ( ExpenseDescription TransactionType Category Amount Currency )
       with updates.

  endmethod.


  method get_reference_data_lists.

    select transactiontype, description from zr_transactiontype into table @DATA(transaction_types).
    loop at transaction_types reference into data(transaction_type).
      result-transaction_types = result-transaction_types &&
        |{ transaction_type->transactiontype } ({ transaction_type->description }),|.
    endloop.

    select category, description from zr_category into table @DATA(categories).
    loop at categories reference into data(category).
      result-categories = result-categories && |{ category->category } ({ category->description }),|.
    endloop.

  endmethod.


  method build_extraction_prompt.

    result = |Analyze the attached receipt and extract the following information.| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |Do NOT wrap the response in markdown. Respond in valid JSON.| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |\{ | && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |"TransactionType" :"",| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |"Category" :"",| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |"ExpenseDescription" :"",| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |"Amount" :"",| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf
          && |"Currency" :""| && cl_abap_char_utilities=>cr_lf

  method call_ai_extraction.

    data(api)               = cl_aic_islm_compl_api_factory=>get( )->create_instance( 'ZINTS_TRAVELAPP' ).
    data(message_container) = api->create_message_container( ).

    message_container->add_user_media_message(
      )->add_media( aic_media_type=>image_webp
      )->set_media_data( cl_web_http_utility=>encode_x_base64( receipt )
      )->add_text( prompt ).

    result = api->execute_for_messages( message_container )->get_completion( ).

  endmethod.

The extraction can be triggered as a RAP determination (automatically when the file is uploaded), as a RAP action (explicitly by the user pressing an "Extract" button), or even through an event-driven side effect that fires after the upload completes. All three options are valid RAP patterns, and the right choice depends on your UX preferences. Personally, I like the determination approach: the user uploads the file, and by the time they look at the form fields, they're already filled in. A small moment of delight in an otherwise tedious process.

Orchestration Adds Enterprise Readiness

This is where the orchestration capabilities mentioned earlier become critical. Receipts may contain sensitive personal data: credit card numbers, home addresses, personal phone numbers. By enabling Data Masking in the orchestration configuration, you ensure that such data is redacted before it reaches the LLM. No code changes required, it's a configuration in the intelligent scenario. Similarly, Document Grounding can be used to provide additional context to the LLM (for example, your company's expense categories and vendor master data), improving extraction accuracy significantly. The LLM doesn't just guess "Restaurant" as a category, it picks the exact category code from your company's chart of accounts.

The Beauty of It

Receipt extraction is a high-volume, low-complexity task that AI handles extremely well. Every minute saved on manual data entry is a minute your employees spend on work that actually matters. And because the extraction runs inside ABAP, not in an external service that your users need to learn, the integration is invisible. The user uploads a file, the fields fill themselves. That's it. That's the entire (very simple) user story.
